headline: Temple Demolished on Private Land: Property Right or Religious Hate Crime?
context: Police arrested four men on 11 Feb 2026 after a partial demolition of the Sri Uchimalai Muniswaran Temple in Rawang. The landowner, Yayasan Kubra, cleared what remained on 25 Feb. On 31 March the High Court lifted a bar on its demolition work.

changes.summary: Correction: The police presence at the 25 Feb clearing is now attributed to CNA, an earlier partial demolition on 11 Feb is added, Penal Code s.295 is described correctly, and an unsourced estimate of 2,500 unregistered temples and other unsourced claims are replaced with sourced figures or removed.

Update: Selangor told its state assembly on 24 April 2026 that 688 Hindu temples operate without approval, 433 on government land and 255 on private land; the card now gives this count in place of the 687 counted at 31 January.

cards.big: A foundation levelled what was left of a Hindu temple on its own land, under police supervision, CNA reported. The High Court later lifted a bar on its demolition work.
cards.sub: Yayasan Kubra cleared the Rawang site on 25 Feb 2026. The temple stood there from 1995; the foundation acquired the land in 2021.

cards.big: Land title is enforceable, but demolishing a temple without court process is not the same as exercising that right.
cards.sub: Police probed the 11 Feb damage under four Penal Code sections, including s.295: damaging a place of worship to insult a religion, or knowing a group will likely take it as an insult.

cards.big: Selangor counted 688 unauthorised Hindu temples in April 2026: 433 on government land and 255 on private land.
cards.sub: A 2015 Malaysia Hindu Sangam survey found 1,577 of 2,251 temples unregistered, an activist told CNA. In February a national committee of Hindu bodies began classifying temples.

cards.big: A group called Tanah Malaya crowdfunded the RM45,000 backhoe used on the temple and said it raised over RM131,000 in a month, CNA reported.
cards.sub: Worshippers at such temples are generally labourers and plantation workers, PSM's S Arutchelvan told CNA. The sites once sat on remote, low-value land, he said.

cards.big: The question is not property versus religion. It is why every party in power since 1965 has chosen inaction, and who profits from the chaos.
Like a squatter settlement where every government promises land titles but nobody ever surveys the plots. The ambiguity serves someone.
cards.sub: Unregistered places of worship exist in legal limbo because formalisation would force decisions no party wants to make

cards.big: Malaysia needs statutory reform for unregistered worship sites, but must confront the class and ethnic power dynamics that make reform politically impossible.
